extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis when evaluating whether a claimed nature-based product limitation is a product-of-nature exception under patent eligibility (Step 2A). Covers when to perform the analysis, how to select natural counterparts, which characteristics to compare, and how to evaluate whether differences are 'marked'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: apply only to nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim to determine whether the nature-based products are 'product of nature' exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a nature-based product can be claimed by itself or as one or more limitations of a claim, care should be taken not to overly extend the markedly different characteristics analysis to products that when viewed as a whole are not nature-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform or skip the analysis for naturally occurring limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and thus falls under the product of nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if the nature-based product limitation is not naturally occurring (for example due to some human intervention), then the markedly different characteristics analysis must be performed to determine whether the claimed product limitation is a product of nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim is to a nature-based product by itself, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire product; where the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components, apply the analysis to the resultant combination; where the claim includes a nature-based product in combination with non-nature-based elements, apply the analysis only to the nature-based product limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a claim to 'a Lactobacillus bacterium' -> analyze entire bacterium (Chakrabarty). A probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk -> analyze the mixture (resultant combination). A yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions -> analyze only the Lactobacillus; container and instructions evaluated separately in Prong Two/Step 2B. See Funk Bros. Seed Co. example where only bacterial mixture was analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For a product-by-process claim, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2113 for more information on product-by-process claims; focus remains on the characteristics of the claimed nature-based product as recited by the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process because the analysis of a process claim should focus on the active steps of the process rather than the products used in those steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited exception: if a process claim is drafted so there is no substantive difference from a product claim (i.e., the claim effectively focuses on the product rather than process steps), then the markedly different analysis applies. Examples: cryopreserving hepatocytes (process focused on steps) vs. claims that effectively claim 'a method of providing an apple' or detecting cffDNA where the claim is directed to the natural product/phenomenon (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; Ariosa/Sequenom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is to select the appropriate counterpart(s) to the nature-based product—i.e., the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state—for comparison in the markedly different characteristics analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, that naturally occurring thing is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A -> acid A). Do not confuse the counterpart with other material that may occur naturally with/adjacent to it (e.g., gene vs. whole chromosome). When multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart(s); for mixtures, compare to the individual nature-based components if no natural mixture exists. Best practice: if the claim is rejected, identify the selected counterpart in the Office action to clarify examiner interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying appropriate characteristics to compare
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify characteristics possessed by the claimed product (as defined by the claim and the broadest reasonable interpretation) to compare against the counterpart. Appropriate characteristics can be expressed as the product's structure, function, and/or other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product, since the claim must define the invention (unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility). Characteristics may be explicitly recited (e.g., chemical name 'deoxyribose') or apparent from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., 'isolated gene B' -> nucleotide sequence, encoded protein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics courts consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting categories of characteristics to consider include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic, physical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided include: protein-encoding information of a nucleic acid (Myriad); ability of complementary nucleotide sequences to bind (Ambry); bacterial infection properties (Funk Bros.); hydrocarbon degradation ability (Chakrabarty); alkalinity, ductility, phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior), presence of plasmids, chemical/crystalline form, nucleotide sequence/genotype, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for determining 'markedly different' characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'markedly different', a characteristic must be changed compared to the naturally occurring counterpart and cannot be an inherent/innate characteristic or an incidental change. The inventor must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and that change was produced by the inventor's efforts/influences, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic such that the claimed product is not a product of nature exception. See Myriad discussion that incidental changes from isolation are not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive examples: products found to have markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples of products held to have markedly different characteristics and thus not products of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified Pseudomonas bacterium with additional plasmids and the functional ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons (structural and functional changes). Myriad: claimed full-length cDNA of BRCA1—structural difference (exons only) though same protein-encoding function—held not a product of nature. These illustrate that structural and/or functional changes produced by the inventor can support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative examples: products lacking markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples where claimed products lacked markedly different characteristics and were treated as products of nature (ineligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolated genes—incidental structural differences from isolation were insufficient because sequences otherwise identical to natural genes. Ambry Genetics: synthetic primers matched natural nucleotide sequences and retained innate DNA functions (binding), so not markedly different. In re Marden: ductility of vanadium was inherent and not a characteristic conferred by a new combination/chemical change. Roslin: cloned farm animals were genetic copies of donors; unclaimed phenotypic differences could not render them markedly different. These illustrate anti-patterns (innate characteristics, incidental changes, unclaimed differences).
